spec: Write a function that takes a list and a list of 0-indexed positions to remove, and returns a new list with the elements at those positions removed, preserving the relative order of the remaining elements. The indices list may be unsorted or contain duplicates; any index that is out of range for the list is simply ignored.

Write a function that inserts a given item into a list after every `interval` elements (interval is a positive integer), but never adds a trailing item after the very last element of the list. For example, inserting 0 into [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with interval 2 produces [1, 2, 0, 3, 4, 0, 5]. Return an empty list if the input list is empty.

Write a function that finds the maximum possible sum of a subset of elements from a list of numbers, subject to the rule that no two chosen elements may be adjacent in the original list. The empty subset (sum 0) is always allowed, which matters when all elements are negative. Return that maximum sum.
Write a function that counts the number of distinct values in a list, regardless of how many times each value repeats. Return 0 for an empty list.

Write a function that computes the running (cumulative) product of a list of numbers: the i-th element of the result is the product of all elements from the start of the list up to and including index i. Return an empty list for an empty input.
Write a function that finds the index of the last occurrence of the maximum value in a non-empty list of numbers. Return that index.
Write a function that computes the arithmetic mean of a non-empty list of numbers and counts how many elements are strictly greater than that mean. Return the count as an integer.

Return a new list containing the elements of the input list with duplicates removed, keeping only the first occurrence of each distinct value and preserving the original relative order. Elements are compared with equality.

Split the list into consecutive chunks of size n, each returned as its own list, preserving the original order of elements. The final chunk may contain fewer than n elements if the list length is not evenly divisible by n. Assume n is a positive integer. An empty list returns an empty list of chunks.

Return a new list that is the input list rotated left by n positions, meaning the first n elements are moved, in the same relative order, to the end of the list. n is a non-negative integer that may exceed the length of the list, in which case it should be treated modulo the list's length. An empty list always returns an empty list, regardless of n.

Return a new list that is the input list rotated right by n positions, meaning the last n elements are moved, in the same relative order, to the front of the list. n is a non-negative integer that may exceed the length of the list, in which case it should be treated modulo the list's length. An empty list always returns an empty list, regardless of n.
Return a new list containing only the even integers from the input list, preserving their original order. Odd integers are excluded, and negative even numbers are treated as even.

Return a list of the values that appear more than once in the input list, each included exactly once in the result, ordered by the position at which that value's second occurrence appears in the input list. If no value repeats, return an empty list.
Group consecutive equal elements of the input list into runs, and return a list of two-element lists [value, count], one per run, in the order the runs occur. An empty list returns an empty list.
Return the second largest distinct value in the input list, where duplicate values only count once when determining distinctness. If the list has fewer than two distinct values, return None.
Return a list of the distinct values from list a that do not appear anywhere in list b, preserving the order in which they first appear in a.
Split a list of integers into two lists, preserving relative order: one containing the even numbers and one containing the odd numbers. Return them together as a tuple (evens, odds).

Given a list of numbers and a positive integer k that is at most the length of the list, return the maximum possible sum of any k consecutive elements in the list. Assume the list has at least k elements.

Return a new list of the same length as the input, where the element at each index is the maximum value seen among the input elements from the start up to and including that index. An empty list returns an empty list.
Return a dictionary mapping each distinct value in the input list to the number of times it appears in that list. An empty list returns an empty dictionary.

Combine two lists by alternating their elements, starting with the first element of a, then the first element of b, then the second element of a, and so on. If one list is longer than the other, append the remaining elements of the longer list to the end, in their original order.
Compute the sum of the decimal digits of an integer n. The sign of n is ignored, so negative numbers use the digits of their absolute value. Zero has a digit sum of 0.
Reverse the decimal digits of an integer n. The sign of n is preserved separately from the digit reversal (e.g. -123 becomes -321), and any leading zeros produced by the reversal are dropped.
Determine whether an integer n reads the same forwards and backwards in decimal. Negative numbers are never palindromes because of the leading minus sign.
Determine whether a positive integer n equals the sum of its proper divisors (all positive divisors of n excluding n itself). Return False for any n less than 1.

For a positive integer n, apply the Collatz process (if even divide by two, if odd multiply by three and add one) repeatedly until reaching 1, and return the total count of numbers in that sequence including both n and the final 1.

For a positive integer n, apply the Collatz process (if even divide by two, if odd multiply by three and add one) repeatedly until reaching 1, and return the largest value that appears anywhere in that sequence, including n itself.

Convert a non-negative or negative integer n into a string representation in the given base (an integer between 2 and 36 inclusive). Use lowercase letters 'a'-'z' for digit values above 9, keep the leading minus sign for negative n, and represent zero as "0".

Parse a string s written in the given base (an integer between 2 and 36 inclusive) into its decimal integer value. The string may use lowercase or uppercase letters for digits above 9 and may have a leading '-' sign.
Compute the greatest common divisor of two integers a and b using their absolute values. If both a and b are 0, return 0.
Compute the least common multiple of two integers a and b using their absolute values. If either a or b is 0, return 0.
Determine whether an integer n is a prime number. Numbers less than 2 are never prime.
Return the n-th prime number, where n is a positive integer and the 1st prime is 2.
Return the list of prime factors of a positive integer n in ascending order, repeated according to multiplicity (for example 12 gives [2, 2, 3]). For n equal to 1, return an empty list.
Return the sorted list of distinct prime numbers that divide a positive integer n. For n equal to 1, return an empty list.
Compute the sum of all positive divisors of a non-negative integer n, including 1 and n itself. If n is 0, return 0.
Return the sorted list of positive divisors of a non-negative integer n that are strictly less than n (so n itself is excluded).
Compute n factorial (the product of all positive integers up to n) for a non-negative integer n. By convention, 0 factorial is 1.
Determine whether an integer n is a perfect square (equal to k*k for some non-negative integer k). Negative numbers are never perfect squares.
Count the number of 1 bits in the binary representation of the absolute value of an integer n.
